Entry 01Data structures

Seven keys, four rotations

Insert the keys 1 to 7 in ascending order. A plain binary search tree would become a chain seven levels deep. The AVL tree rotates four times and finishes with three levels.

Original drawing

Lab 01 · Insertion replay

step=7

1234567

Ascending keys always land at the far right, so every imbalance is the right-right case and a single left rotation repairs it. Nodes keep their left-to-right order; rotations only change depth.

After inserting keys 1 through 7, the root is 4 and the tree has three levels.

Entry 02C++17 benchmark

How tall does a tree grow?

My C++ benchmark feeds the same sequence of keys to an AVL tree, a red-black tree and a splay tree. Change the insertion order to see which trees keep their depth, then compare how long each batch took.

Recorded run · DS_Actual_CP @ b80db89

Lab 02 · Tree benchmark

order=ascending · size=10000 · metric=height

Random keys use seed 42 and can repeat. Ordered inputs use each integer from 1 to the selected size once.

At 10,000 ascending insertions, the splay tree has one level per key. The AVL tree reaches 14 levels.

Single run. Each configuration has one recorded run; every timing is one measurement, not an average.

Source Recorded data (metrics.json at commit b80db89, opens external site) Runner L32–55 (BenchmarkRunner.cpp, opens external site) Seed 42 generator (DatasetGenerator.cpp, opens external site)

Final height in levels, ascending keys
Tree1,0005,00010,000
AVL101314
Red-black172224
Splay1,0005,00010,000
How the measurements were taken

Each configuration has one recorded run. Height counts levels, with a single node at level one. Time covers the full insertion batch and excludes key generation and height measurement. Random inputs use seed 42 and can repeat keys. Ordered inputs use each integer from 1 through the selected size once.

In the ascending workload, each new key is the largest. Splaying moves it to the root, with the previous tree on its left. Repeating that step creates the chain visible in the height measurements.

The source project records 375 runs: five trees, five operations, five datasets and three sizes. This page plots the 27 insert runs for AVL, red-black and splay trees on ascending, random and descending keys. The values match the source file exactly.

Entry 03Information retrievalCollaborator’s repository

Which review surfaces first?

In Review Summarizer, a team project with Niraj Chavan (repository maintained by Niraj), one search ranks product reviews by keywords and another by meaning. Reciprocal rank fusion combines their positions into a single result.

Illustrative · fictional reviews

Lab 03 · Rank fusion

scenario=overlap · channel=hybrid

Illustrative reviews for a search about battery life.

Scoresum of 1 / (60 + rank)Rank starts at 1. A review missing from a list gets nothing from it.

Commute leads. Commute receives 1/62 + 1/62 = 0.03226.

Source hybrid_search.py L63–77 (collaborator’s repository at commit 68d0c0a, opens external site)

Where the rankings come from

The repository includes a retriever that fuses BM25 keyword ranks with FAISS and multilingual-E5 semantic ranks. The example uses three fictional headphone reviews with assigned ranks. Each match contributes 1/(60 + rank) to the score, and a review missing from a list receives zero from that list.

Rank fusion compares positions instead of raw scores, so BM25 scores never have to be calibrated against cosine similarity. When two reviews tie, the semantic list’s order decides, as in the source’s stable sort.

Limitations: the reviews are fictional, and the fusion step is not on the served path of the source app.

Read the three sample reviews
